To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(a) DNA.Land can be used to create genome/phenome databases at a small fraction of the cost of traditional studies; and (b) the resulting databases are of high quality, as evidenced by their ability to identify rare variants and their high level of concordance with traditional data sets.

DNA.Land: a) is a framework for collecting genomes and phenomes from individuals tested by consumer genomic companies, b) has collected 1,200 genomes, 1,000 of whom have consented to participate, and c) has a high rate of participation from individuals of European descent, and a low rate of participation from African-Americans.

DNA.Land has collected over 100,000 genomes from 60,000 individuals, that the genomes are highly diverse and include a large fraction of individuals of non-European ancestry, and that we have developed a new framework for collecting and analyzing phenotypic information from individuals who have not been previously studied.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the intersection of genomics, social science, and computer science.

the ethical, legal, and social issues that arise from the use of personal genetic information, the collection and use of genomes and phenomes for scientific research, and the development of technologies that enable these uses.
the collection, analysis, and sharing of personal genomics data.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
DNA.Land is a digital biobanking platform that collects genetic data from individuals tested by consumer genomic companies using a small fraction of the resources needed by traditional studies.
the study of the DNA.Land is an excellent example of how to use the power of crowdsourcing to collect data for scientific research.
DNA.Land is the first digital biobank for genetic data.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
we have developed a platform that collects data from individuals who are already interested in their own data.
DNA.Land is an example of how the internet and social networks can enable large-scale data collection.
DNA.Land is a platform for the public to contribute their genetic and phenotypic data to science.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the DNA.Land framework can be used to collect genome/phenome data at scale.
it is possible to create a genome/phenome collection that is comparable to those of traditional studies using a fraction of their resources.
we can create genome/phenome collections that are large enough to be statistically meaningful, and do so in a way that respects the privacy of individuals.
